blocks.text: I can investigate the extension of a rubber band, and compare the behaviour to that of a spring.
Does a rubber band stretch in the same way as a spring? You will find out.

items.title: Measuring the extension of a rubber band

blocks.text: Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: The extension of a rubber band is its change in length.
A rubber band is elastic; it returns to its original length after forces are removed from it.
Variables are directly proportional when one is a constant multiple of the other.
Rubber contains long molecular chains, that uncoil when it stretches.

blocks.text: A rubber band gets longer when you put a force on it, just like a spring. But there are differences.

items: A spring stays the same thickness and just gets longer.
A rubber band gets **thinner** as it gets longer. The more force, the thinner it gets.
Both return to their original length and size when the force is removed. This is {elastic} behaviour.

blocks.text: We investigate a rubber band the same way as a spring: hang it up, hang masses from it to make a constant downward force, and measure the extension. The extension is how much longer the band has become.

The question: is the extension of a rubber band {directly proportional} to the force on it? When you double the force, does the extension double? A spring does this, but we do not yet know about a rubber band.

blocks.q: Which prediction is about the extension being directly proportional to the force?
options: The rubber band will get thinner as you add force
If the force doubles, the extension will double
The rubber band will look shiny
The rubber band will get warmer
blocks.why: Directly proportional means that doubling the force doubles the extension.

blocks.q: A pupil predicts: There is no extension when there is no force pulling on the band. Is this consistent with the extension being directly proportional to the force?
blocks.why: In a directly proportional relationship, no force means no extension.

blocks.text: Hang the rubber band from a clamp stand and put a vertical ruler beside it, with the ruler’s zero exactly level with the bottom of the band.

A rubber band is loose, so it is harder to find its bottom than for a spring. Do not stretch it! Gently pull down on the band with a second ruler to find its natural length, keep that ruler horizontal, and line it up with the zero on the vertical ruler.

blocks.q: Why do you gently pull down on the rubber band with a second ruler before measuring?
options: To stretch it as far as possible
To find its natural length without stretching it, so the zero can be lined up
To add a force of 1 N
blocks.why: The band is loose, so this technique finds its natural (unstretched) length to line up with zero.

items: Set up the equipment with zero on the ruler in line with the bottom of the rubber band.
Hang a mass hanger on the band and measure the extension.
Add masses one at a time and measure the extension for each.

blocks.text: Record the force and extension in a table, then plot extension against force. Your values will be different from others, but the pattern should be the same.
A typical graph for a rubber band is a smooth {S-shaped curve}. Do not draw a straight line of best fit through the points.
Conclusion: the extension is NOT directly proportional to the force, because the line is not a straight line. This is different from a spring.

slides.title: Which line is a rubber band?

blocks.q: Which graph of extension against force is typical for a rubber band?
options: A straight line through the origin
A straight line that goes downwards
blocks.why: Rubber bands give a smooth S-shaped curve, so the extension is not directly proportional to the force.

blocks.text: The band behaves differently depending on the size of the force.

blocks.q: Match each part of the graph to how the band behaves.

blocks.text: To compare two sections, look at the extra stretch for each extra newton. A bigger extra stretch per newton means the band is easier to stretch there.

slides.title: Which part is easier to stretch?

blocks.q: Going from 2 N to 3 N stretches a rubber band by an extra 1.0 cm. Going from 5 N to 6 N stretches it by an extra 3.0 cm. Where is the band easier to stretch?
blocks.why: An extra 3.0 cm for one more newton is a bigger stretch than 1.0 cm, so the band is easier to stretch there.

slides.title: Why does rubber behave this way?

blocks.text: A spring’s coils move apart evenly when you pull, so a spring stretches in proportion to the force.
Rubber contains {long chains of molecules}. Normally these chains are coiled up together.

items: A small force starts to uncoil the chains, but this does not cause much stretching.
Larger forces make the chains line up more easily, so the band stretches more easily.
Near their maximum length the chains can hardly stretch any more, so the band is hard to stretch again.

blocks.q: Which part of the rubber band graph does each explanation belong to?

items.text: The long chains of molecules are coiled together
The molecule chains are able to straighten out
The chains have straightened and cannot stretch much more

blocks.q: Why does a rubber band stretch differently from a spring?
options: It is made from a softer material, and that is the whole reason
Its long molecular chains behave differently from metal coils
blocks.why: The long molecular chains in rubber uncoil in stages, which gives the S-shaped curve. A spring’s coils just move apart evenly.

items.q: A rubber band is 7.0 cm long unloaded and 11.5 cm long with a force on it. What is its extension?
What happens to the width of a rubber band as you stretch it?
What does it mean that a rubber band is elastic?
options: It returns to its original length when the force is removed
Its extension is directly proportional to the force

items: The extension of a rubber band is not proportional to the force on it, but rubber is elastic.
A rubber band is hard to stretch at first, then easier to stretch, then hard to stretch again (an S-shaped graph).
The behaviour of rubber is explained by the uncoiling of long molecular chains.
A spring stretches in proportion to the force (Hooke’s law), and a rubber band does not.

flashcards.front: What happens to the thickness of a rubber band when it is stretched?
flashcards.back: It gets thinner as it gets longer. (A spring stays the same thickness.)
The material returns to its original length after the forces are removed.

flashcards.front: What is the extension of a rubber band?
flashcards.back: Its change in length (how much longer it has become).
One variable is a constant multiple of the other: doubling the force would double the extension.

flashcards.front: Is the extension of a rubber band directly proportional to the force on it?
flashcards.back: No. The graph is not a straight line.

flashcards.front: What shape is the graph of extension against force for a rubber band?
flashcards.back: A smooth S-shaped curve. Do not draw a straight line through it.

flashcards.front: Describe how a rubber band stretches as the force increases.
flashcards.back: Hard to stretch at first, then easier to stretch, then hard to stretch again.

flashcards.front: What structure in rubber explains its stretching pattern?
flashcards.back: Long molecular chains, which uncoil when the band stretches.

flashcards.front: Why is a rubber band hard to stretch at first?
flashcards.back: The long molecular chains are coiled together. A small force only starts to uncoil them.

flashcards.front: Why does a rubber band become hard to stretch again at large forces?
flashcards.back: The molecular chains have straightened and are close to their maximum length.

flashcards.front: How do you find the natural length of the band before measuring?
flashcards.back: Gently pull down on it with a second ruler, without stretching it, and line that ruler up with the zero on the vertical ruler.

flashcards.front: How does a spring stretch differently from a rubber band?
flashcards.back: A spring’s extension is directly proportional to the force (Hooke’s law): its coils move apart evenly. A rubber band’s is not.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Stretching rubber
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a word, a number or a short phrase. Give units where they are asked for.

questions.prompt: What happens to the thickness of a rubber band as you stretch it: does it get thicker, thinner or stay the same?
questions.explanation: A rubber band becomes thinner as it gets longer.

questions.prompt: What word describes a material that returns to its original length after the force is removed?
questions.explanation: Rubber bands and springs are elastic.

questions.prompt: A rubber band is 7.0 cm long unloaded and 11.5 cm long when a force acts on it. What is its extension? Give your answer in cm.
A mass hanger gives a force of 1 N and each 100 g mass adds 1 N. What is the total force with a hanger and 3 masses? Give your answer in newtons.
Is the extension of a rubber band directly proportional to the force on it? Answer yes or no.
questions.explanation: The graph is an S-shaped curve, not a straight line through the origin.

questions.prompt: What shape is the line of best fit for a typical rubber band graph of extension against force?
questions.explanation: The curve is a smooth S shape, so a straight line should not be drawn.

questions.prompt: What structure inside rubber explains how it stretches? Give a short phrase.
questions.explanation: Long molecular chains uncoil as the band stretches.

questions.prompt: On the S-shaped graph, is the rubber band easier or harder to stretch in the middle part than at the start?
questions.explanation: The molecule chains are able to straighten out, so the band stretches more easily there.

questions.prompt: Going from 2 N to 3 N a rubber band stretches an extra 1.0 cm; going from 5 N to 6 N it stretches an extra 3.0 cm. Which force change is where the band is easier to stretch: 2 N to 3 N or 5 N to 6 N?
questions.explanation: A bigger extra stretch for each newton means the band is easier to stretch there.
